data.title: CANADA STOCKS-TSX rises as resource stocks gain; markets weigh BoC outlook
data.description:
Oct 16 (Reuters) - Canada's main stock index climbed to a more-than-one-month high on Friday, led by gains in materials and energy shares, while investors assessed Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem's warning on persistent energy-price pressures on interest rates.

The S&P/TSX Composite Index rose 0.8% to 36,406.48 points at 10:30 a.m. ET, its highest level since September 4. It was on track for a second consecutive weekly gain.

* The materials sector advanced 1% after prices of gold and silver rose

* Brent crude fell 0.4% but remained above $100 a barrel, keeping attention on the energy sector, which rose 1.2% on Friday and is up more than 60% so far this year

* Strength in commodity-linked shares helped lift the resource-heavy Canadian benchmark after a sharp, AI-driven technology selloff rattled global markets earlier this week, with a more limited impact on the TSX

* "Materials, gold in particular, and copper, we're pretty bullish on those materials sectors. That could help TSX go higher," said Michael Dehal, a senior portfolio manager at Dehal Investment Partners at Raymond James

* Dehal said the index would be particularly sensitive to developments in the Middle East and movements in bond yields

* Macklem said Canada has not raised interest rates yet but the longer elevated energy prices go on "the harder that gets"

* The BoC is not expected to raise interest rates at its next monetary policy decision announcement on October 28, but money markets are pricing in a rate hike of 25 basis points in December, according to data compiled by LSEG

* Data on the day showed that Canadian home sales extended their decline in September, after a drop in August, as higher mortgage rates and expectations of a rate hike weighed on demand

* The consumer discretionary sector climbed 0.8%, led by Aritzia ( ATZAF ) rising 1.2% after Scotiabank resumed coverage with a 'sector outperform' rating

(Reporting by Anand Gopal in Bengaluru; Editing by Shreya Biswas)

data.title: Netflix Taking Significant Steps to Address Engagement Issues, Wedbush Says
data.description:
10:55 AM EDT, 10/16/2026 (MT Newswires) -- Netflix ( NFLX ) is making significant changes to address slowing viewer engagement and revive growth, though the benefits may take time to materialize, Wedbush Securities said in a Friday note.

Netflix ( NFLX ) faces modestly declining viewer engagement as consumers spend more time on YouTube and short-form social media, according to Wedbush. However, the streaming company's large subscriber base, low churn rates and extensive content library continue to make it an attractive platform for advertisers, the brokerage said.

Late Thursday, Netflix ( NFLX ) announced the appointment of Peter Rice as its new chief content officer, effective Oct. 26. Rice most recently served as chairman of Walt Disney Television and chairman of general entertainment at Walt Disney ( DIS ) , overseeing Fox Broadcasting, Fox Sports and several other businesses.

Wedbush believes Rice's experience at Fox and Disney ( DIS ) could help Netflix ( NFLX ) pursue a potential studio acquisition or expand its theatrical business and broader entertainment offerings.

Netflix ( NFLX ) plans to lay off about 1,000 employees, or 6% of its workforce, amid growing competition for viewers from traditional rivals and YouTube, Reuters reported earlier in the week.

"Concerns have lingered since Netflix ( NFLX ) reported (second-quarter) earnings, and Netflix ( NFLX ) has recently made significant changes to address them and shift the business in a direction that could reinvigorate profitable growth," Wedbush analyst Alicia Reese wrote.

Wedbush analysts believe that Netflix's ( NFLX ) ad revenue remains on track to double to roughly $3 billion this year, as the brokerage reiterated its outperform rating on the stock ahead of the release of the company's third-quarter results on Tuesday. However, it trimmed the price target to $90 from $105.

Netflix's ( NFLX ) second-quarter results released in July showed revenue fell short of Wall Street's estimates, while the company said it will no longer publish its engagement report semi-annually.

Wedbush expects third-quarter earnings per share of $0.83, surpassing the consensus of $0.82 that matches management's guidance. The brokerage is looking at revenue of $12.87 billion, compared with consensus of $12.88 billion and guidance for $12.86 billion.

Shares of Netflix ( NFLX ) were down 2.1% in Friday trade, taking its year-to-date losses to 24%. The company is scheduled to announce its third-quarter results on Oct. 20.

data.title: NY Fed service sector survey finds notable price pressures
data.description:
Oct 16 (Reuters) - Service sector business leaders reported widespread pricing woes in October and a downbeat outlook for activity, according to a report released Friday by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

"The pace of input price increases remained sharp, and selling price increases picked up to the fastest pace since 2022," the bank said in its latest Business Leaders Survey for the current month, adding "supply availability continued to worsen."

The price pressures faced by the company leaders came as the report found that the business climate was "much worse than normal" with firms becoming more pessimistic about the outlook. Current business activity also weakened, with the headline index dropping 12 points to negative 20.7, the weakest reading since March, the report said.

The sour mood captured by the New York Fed survey contrasts with other data that shows strong economic activity, low and steady unemployment and robust levels of investment tied to the technology sector.

That said, the survey's downbeat findings on inflation mirror a raft of statistics showing price pressures remain strong amid the ongoing impact of President Donald Trump's trade tariffs and the US-Israeli war in the Middle East that's driven surging energy costs.

High inflation drove the Fed to hike rates last month and it's very likely to do so again by year's end, though in comments late Thursday, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh offered no guidance, saying "I don't prejudge meetings...I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year."

Chicago Fed leader Austan Goolsbee, in a Yahoo Finance interview on Wednesday, said a consumer level inflation report released on Wednesday was "discouraging" and noted "if you break out the components, services inflation shows little sign of improvement."

"We're going to need to keep a close eye" on that part of the price pressure landscape "because that's not really coming from supply shocks," Goolsbee said.

The NY Fed survey pointing to rough price pressures came as the government reported a surge in import prices in September, with those costs rising by a much bigger than expected 1.1% rate.

The Business Leaders survey also pointed to "weak" capital spending plans and while noting "supply availability is expected to continue to worsen."

The sour turn in the October Business Leaders survey, joined with other regional data from the bank, points to an uneven environment in the New York area. The bank's October Empire State factory survey, released Thursday, saw the overall business conditions index rise to its highest level in five years amid "elevated" input and selling prices and supply-related challenges.

(Reporting by Michael S. Derby; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama )

data.title: US manufacturing output rises in September
data.description:
WASHINGTON, Oct 16 (Reuters) - US factory production increased in September, but lost considerable momentum in the third quarter amid headwinds from the Middle East conflict, which has snarled supply chains and raised energy prices. 

Manufacturing output rebounded 0.3% last month following a revised 0.2% decline in August, the Federal Reserve said on Friday. The rise was in line with economists' expectations. Factory production was previously estimated to have dropped 0.3% in August. Output advanced 1.1% on a year-over-year basis in September. It grew at a 0.7% annualized rate in the third quarter after accelerating at a 5.6% pace in the second quarter.

Manufacturing accounts for about 9.4% of the economy. While an AI infrastructure buildout and businesses rebuilding inventories to meet robust domestic demand are supporting factory activity, higher energy prices, a trade war with Canada and rising borrowing costs pose downside risks to production. 

Diesel prices have surged to a record high as the US-Israeli war with Iran drags on, and economists say the economy could soon feel the effects through higher prices for goods, including at the supermarket, which could weigh on demand.

Durable goods manufacturing production edged up 0.1%, lifted by gains in the output of primary metals, machinery, and electrical equipment, appliances and components. Production of motor vehicles and parts fell 3.0%. Durable goods manufacturing output increased at a 3.8% rate in the third quarter, partly boosted by a 28.4% surge in the production of semiconductors and related electronic components related to the AI spending boom.

Nondurable manufacturing production rose 0.4% over the month amid gains in printing and chemicals output. Nondurable manufacturing output, however, fell 1.6% last quarter.  

Mining production rose 0.2% last month and grew at a 5.0% rate in the July-September quarter. Utilities jumped 3.5% amid demand for air-conditioning. Utilities output increased at a 14.8% pace in the third quarter.

Overall industrial production rose 0.7% last month after gaining 0.1% in August. Industrial output increased 2.2% year-on-year in September. It advanced at a 2.8% pace in the third quarter after growing at a 4.8% rate in the second quarter.

Capacity utilization for the industrial sector, a measure of how fully firms are using their resources, rose to 76.9% last month from 76.4% in August. It is 2.5 percentage points below its 1972-2025 average. The operating rate for the manufacturing sector edged up to 75.9% from 75.8% in August. It is 2.3 percentage points below its long-run average.

(Reporting by Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Andrea Ricci )

data.title: ExxonMobil signals $4.5 billion refining earnings boost as margins soar
data.description:
Oct 16 (Reuters) - ExxonMobil ( XOM ) signaled on Friday that higher refining margins during the third quarter could boost its downstream profit by $4.5 billion compared with the previous three months.

Refining margins have soared due to the ongoing Iran war, which has restricted energy exports through the Strait of Hormuz, as well as Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. The resulting higher fuel prices have created political risks for the administration of US President Donald Trump ahead of the midterm elections in November.

The top US oil producer's expected refining boom could further draw the ire of the president, who complained in August that Exxon and Chevron ( CVX ) were making "too much money".

Exxon's regulatory filing indicates that adjusted net income for the refining business could jump to $8.5 billion, wrote BMO Capital Markets analyst Phillip Jungwirth in a research note. That would be more than double last quarter's profit level.

Here are more details from Exxon's earnings preview:

-- Upstream earnings could take a $1.3 billion hit compared with the second quarter. The average closing Brent benchmark price declined about 5.6% during the third quarter compared with the previous three months, according to LSEG data.

-- Exxon indicated that there were no volume-related disruptions during the quarter stemming from the Iran war.

-- The company's move to divest some upstream assets will boost earnings by $700 million.

-- Exxon will release full third-quarter results on October 30.

-- Exxon shares were up less than 1% in pre-market trading.

(Reporting by Sheila Dang in Houston and Dharna Bafna in Bengaluru; Editing by Anil D'Silva, Joe Bavier and Chizu Nomiyama)

data.title: NG Energy International Releases Results From Aruchara-6 Well in Colombia
data.description:
10:05 AM EDT, 10/16/2026 (MT Newswires) -- NG Energy International ( GASXF ) released initial results from the Aruchara-6 well at its Maria Conchita Block in Colombia, and provided an operational update on the Sinu-9 Block.

The company said Friday that Aruchara-6 well has been drilled, completed and connected to the central processing facility at Maria Conchita, with well performance evaluation now underway through the CPF and new gas volumes being sold into the Colombian marketplace.

The well produced at rates of up to 8.7 million cubic feet per day (MMcf/d) gross (6.96 MMcf/d net) during initial flow tests done through the CPF, with a choke of 30/64 and average tubing head pressure of 780 pounds per square inch (psi), said the company.

The company expects the total field production at Maria Conchita with the addition of this well to increase to 23.0 MMcf/d gross (18.4 MMcf/d net), compared to 16.0 MMcf/d gross (12.8 MMcf/d net) prior to the addition of the well, bringing the combined company net production across Maria Conchita and Sinu-9 to approximately 29.1 MMcf/d, it said.

At the Sinu-9 Block, the Encantado-1X well was spudded on Oct 6, and drilling is currently underway, the company said. Commissioning of the Sinu-9 pipeline loop is now complete, increasing gross transportation capacity to 40-45 MMcf/d (15.6-17.6 MMcf/d net), NG said.

“Noor’s extensive experience leading global risk and underwriting functions at Citibank and Barclays makes him an outstanding addition to SEDA. His deep knowledge of counterparty credit risk, market risk, fund structures, and financing transactions will be invaluable to clients facing complex disputes and regulatory matters,” said Damiano Colnago, Managing Partner of SEDA Experts.

Noor Ul Islam is a trading and risk management expert with almost 30 years experience of working in trading and banking across global financial asset and product markets. This includes serving as Global Head of Counterparty Credit Underwriting at Citi Wealth Management and holding numerous global risk leadership roles at Barclays, as well as being Head of Trading for Fund Linked products at both Swiss Re and Dresdner Bank. His expertise spans structured derivative products and equity-linked financing, counterparty credit risk, market risk, fund derivatives, CIUs including mutual and hedge funds as well as family offices, prime services, and emerging markets.

Dr. Islam most recently served as Global Head of Counterparty Credit Underwriting at Citi Wealth Management, where he led a global team of more than 80 professionals responsible for counterparty credit assessment and approval across structured lending and derivatives. His remit covered private banking, institutional family office, and retail clients across the United States, UAE, Singapore, and Hong Kong.

At Citi, Dr. Islam also led major regulatory-driven transformation initiatives within Wealth counterparty credit, including the implementation of new Wholesale Credit Risk requirements. He helped redesign underwriting processes, governance, and supporting systems, held approval authority for financing exposures, developed Citi Wealth’s first comprehensive close-out framework, and established its Institutional Family Office underwriting framework.

Previously, Dr. Islam spent 12 years at Barclays within the Corporate and Investment Bank Risk function, where he held transactional approval authority and significant regulatory, policy, and limit-setting responsibilities across multiple businesses. He also regularly represented Barclays in meetings with its lead regulators.

At Barclays, Dr. Islam held several senior global risk leadership roles, including Global Head of Equity Linked Financing Risk, Global Head of Fund Structures Risk, Global Head of ETF Risk, Deputy Global Head of Equity Market Risk, and Head of Risk for Barclays Investment Management. He also held senior responsibility for Prime Services, structured transactions, emerging markets, and principal investments.

Earlier in his career, Dr. Islam served as Head of Trading, Managed Account & Fund Derivatives at Swiss Re, with global responsibility for fund derivatives and financing products out of London and New York, as well as the development of the firm’s managed account platform. data.title: Fed's Warsh sees US resilience, mum on rate-path view
data.description:
BANGKOK, Oct 16 (Reuters) - Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh voiced optimism on Friday about US economic strength and surprise about how well global economies have been "hanging in there" amid continued energy shocks and tighter monetary policy to fight inflation.

He said the US and many other economies were benefiting from an "investment surge" driven by artificial intelligence but broadening to other sectors that was creating a near-term demand shock that was putting upward pressure on inflation.

"I came out of meetings here yesterday and today and it's hard to be in a discussion with central bankers and not compare notes and hear the same thing about the surge in prices," Warsh said at the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.

With inflation a "common challenge," Warsh said global central banks undertook "a synchronous tightening in monetary policy in most places around the world, and that means there's no free riders."

In the US, he said, "We made very clear that we would deliver price stability, and we removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago," in a reference to the Fed's September interest-rate hike. 

NO PREVIEW OF RATE PATH

But in keeping with his style since taking the reins as Fed chief in May, he gave no preview about whether he feels more interest-rate hikes will be needed, or when.

"I don't prejudge meetings," Warsh added in the discussion with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva. "I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year."

Warsh's colleagues at the Fed have not been reticent on their rate-path views.

In recent weeks nearly all said they feel more tightening is probably needed, but most wanted to see more economic data in order to assess the inflation trend, a signal that they were unlikely to deliver a second rate hike this month.

Financial markets have taken those remarks on board and are betting the Fed will wait until December to raise rates.

That remained true even after reports this week showed two different measures of inflation running higher than expected and heading in the wrong direction from the Fed's 2% goal.

Warsh's decision to skirt the near-term policy decision altogether and stick to broader economic themes leaves intact the expectation that the Fed will not hike this month.

'BUMPY' AI PATH TO MORE WEALTH

Warsh was optimistic about the impact of AI on economic growth and productivity in the medium-term, even as he said it would be a "very bumpy" path toward what he expected would be faster productivity growth in the "real economy" that would bolster wealth.

"It's obviously hitting the demand side of the economy before it's going to hit the supply side of the economy," he said. "We don't know in the next 12 or 18 months its effect on employment, but if you believe like I believe, which is it will make economies and countries that put it to good use more productive, that it's going to make it so that we will have more wealth, then that has to be a very good thing."

A task force convened to advise the Fed on the impact of AI on productivity and jobs will hold a "field hearing" in the San Francisco Bay Area on November 16, he said, in what will be a first public peek at the group's work.

EMERGING STRONGER

He said a broadening of the investment surge beyond AI was providing some resilience to US growth.

"It means we've got plenty of tailwinds that are giving some strength and durability to this economy," he said. "That sort of momentum is certainly not found everywhere in the world."  

But the global economy, too, was "showing resilience that I'm not sure I would have predicted five or six months ago, given what's happening in geopolitics and hotspots around the world."

The IMF earlier this week said that AI investment would keep global growth above 3% this year, partly offsetting the drag from oil prices that are hovering above $100 per barrel, but risks from high debt loads and a potential sharp pullback in AI investment and asset values threaten the outlook.

Warsh said that central bankers meeting in Bangkok had a common vision to safeguard price stability and were taking action to back that view, which was giving "confidence to businesses and households that's so important for growth to continue."

"I believe optimistically - you might think naively - at least in the United States, we're going to come out of this stronger with a more durable economy, more capable of leading the world on economic growth," Warsh said.

(Writing by Ann Saphir and David Lawder; Editing by Christian Schmollinger, Clarence Fernandez, Toby Chopra)

data.title: CoreWeave bond rout tests market's math on AI buildout
data.description:
PROVIDENCE, Rhode Island/NEW YORK, Oct 16 (Reuters) - A sharp decline in CoreWeave's ( CRWV ) bonds this week is emerging as a test of investors' willingness to keep financing the massive buildout of AI infrastructure, as rising borrowing costs and scrutiny of debt-funded expansion hit the sector.

Analysts and portfolio managers said the selloff in the data center operator's debt carries more significance than a concurrent rout in its shares because it may signal a broader reassessment of the risks tied to financing AI projects that may take years to generate revenue.

CoreWeave ( CRWV ) bonds issued in June at a yield of 9.675% have plunged in value, sending their yield to 15% this week.

"CoreWeave ( CRWV ) is absolutely the canary in the coal mine" for a market segment that is coming under more stress, said Max Frumes, global head of distressed and leveraged finance at 9fin, a fintech corporate credit data and analytics company.

"This is going to be a turning point in the pricing and availability and structure of credit that's supporting the AI boom," said Frumes, who believes that other AI-linked debt will follow CoreWeave ( CRWV ) into distressed territory. "It's going to get more expensive. There will be a lot more scrutiny and probably some pushback from investors."

CoreWeave ( CRWV ) shares fell 15.1% from Monday's open through Thursday's close, despite a 6% gain on Thursday after a vote of confidence from partner Nvidia. The decline was broadly in line with weakness in other so-called neocloud companies such as Nebius and Iren.

Credit investors said they already are becoming more selective.

"We're definitely taking another look at our exposures across the AI infrastructure space, particularly where the risks are concentrated and whether we're being adequately compensated for taking them," said John Han, a portfolio manager at fixed-income asset management firm F/m Investments.

F/m's portfolio contains unsecured CoreWeave ( CRWV ) bonds in one of its exchange-traded funds, but only because they make up part of the index tracked by the ETF. At their current yields those bonds "certainly deserve another look," Han said. He generally prefers to invest in high-yield securities via special purpose vehicles that may offer lower yields but also more collateral and less risk.

"The market is being very selective and really singling out anything that has more leverage, and (that may be) in a bit more challenging operating environment," said Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager of fixed income at Catalyst funds.

To Holzenthaler and other investors, what the markets are witnessing now is an overreaction as sentiment shifts from being overly upbeat to downright bearish.

In June, the risks driving the selloff -- the sheer size of the funding needs, the leverage, the reliance on outside financing, the risk that the GPUs (graphics processing units) being purchased for data centers would be obsolete before the new facilities could open -- were merely overlooked or downplayed.

"A few months ago, I would have said people were just too optimistic around AI," Holzenthaler said.

Deutsche Bank global head of macro and thematic research Jim Reid sees the market entering a new phase in which debt financing is becoming increasingly important.

"As we move to a capex cycle funded out of debt rather than simply free cash flow, we have to increasingly respect the credit price action," Reid wrote in a recent report. "AI financing costs aren't dramatic overall, but there are worrying themes at the edges."

Vanguard bond portfolio manager Brad Collins said assessing AI-related debt has become more challenging as issuers bring increasingly large and varied offerings to market, often forcing investors to make decisions in days or even hours.

Rising inflation has pushed financing costs higher overall and fueled concern about what lies ahead for mammoth AI capital spending plans. Then there is the growing political controversy surrounding the construction of data centers.

Even one of the tech sector's stalwarts allows that the road ahead may be bumpy at times. Dan Ives, partner and technology analyst at Yorkville Ives, an investment firm, estimates that 5% to 10% of planned projects ultimately will not be built.

"The growing noise around data center permitting and midterm rhetoric on power prices has given investors another reason to step back," Ives said.

(Reporting by Suzanne McGee in Providence, Rhode Island and Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss in New York; editing by Colin Barr and Cynthia Osterman)

data.title: Private credit roundup: CoreWeave's debt stress tests private credit's AI financing boom
data.description:
Oct 16 (Reuters) - Private credit's expanding role in financing AI infrastructure faced one of its clearest market tests this week as CoreWeave's bonds fell to distressed levels, raising questions about how lenders are pricing a boom built on chips, data centres and customer contracts.

CoreWeave has about $50 billion of debt, according to LSEG data, making it one of the largest borrowers linking private credit to the AI buildout.

The cost of insuring its debt against default climbed to about 1,200 basis points this week, while yields on some of its bonds rose to roughly 15% to 16%, signalling sharply increased investor concern over its credit risk.

James Martin, senior US credit strategist at SMBC, said investors were favoring high-yield data-centre financings for projects closer to completion and with fewer hurdles before entering service.

"There is still a price. Investors are still comfortable financing it, but they're demanding more compensation for it," he said, referring to projects further from completion.

Private capital has played a central role in CoreWeave's expansion.

It raised a $2.3 billion facility in 2023 backed by graphics processing units, or GPUs, led by Magnetar Capital and Blackstone Tactical Opportunities, followed by a $7.5 billion facility in 2024 involving Blackstone, Magnetar, Carlyle, BlackRock and other investors.

An $8.5 billion facility raised in March this year was anchored by Blackstone Credit & Insurance.

The implications extend well beyond one borrower.

Alternative asset manager Carlyle said in an October paper that private credit could be called on to finance roughly $1 trillion of the AI-compute buildout, more than half the industry's current assets under management.

It warned that rapid lending into the sector could create concentration risks similar to those that emerged in software lending.

"The clearest lesson is not to avoid AI compute exposure, but to set concentration limits before the buildout accelerates further, not after," Carlyle said.

Some AI loans are backed not only by GPUs but also by long-term customer contracts.

CoreWeave has large commitments from Microsoft, OpenAI and Meta Platforms, while several of its financings use special-purpose vehicles tied to specific infrastructure assets and customer contracts.

That can strengthen the credit by reducing lenders' reliance on the resale value of chips, but it can also create concentration risk if repayment depends heavily on a small number of large customers continuing to honour and renew those contracts.

If funding costs remain elevated, lenders could demand wider spreads, lower leverage, stronger covenants and tighter limits on customer and technology concentration.

Direct-lending funds raised $129.15 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 35% from a year earlier and the highest nine-month total in Preqin data going back to 2016.

Estimated third-quarter lending volume, however, fell 28% year on year to $49.77 billion, according to PitchBook/LCD.

Competition from the syndicated loan market has also intensified.

Some $16.39 billion of direct-lending loans were refinanced in the broadly syndicated market in the third quarter, compared with just $2.60 billion of syndicated loans moving into direct lending, PitchBook/LCD data showed.

(Reporting By Patturaja Murugaboopathy; with additional reporting by Vidya Ranganathan; Editing by Vijay Kishore)

* Futures: Dow down 0.04%, S&P up 0.04%, Nasdaq down 0.28%

* Tesla, SpaceX gain after unveiling redesigned Roadster

* Chips, neocloud companies slip again in premarket trading

(Updates with prices)

By Tharuniyaa Lakshmi and Purvi Agarwal

Oct 16 (Reuters) - US stock index futures were muted on Friday, as technology stocks came under fresh pressure on worries about cracks building in the AI trade, though a rise in Tesla shares and decline in oil prices offered support.

The electric vehicle maker rose 3% in premarket trading after unveiling a redesigned Roadster, powered by rocket-style thrusters, developed in collaboration with SpaceX.

Elon Musk's rocket and space technology company gained 1.2%.

Cautionary signs persisted in the AI sector as Nvidia-backed CoreWeave ( CRWV ) slipped 5.2%, after Thursday's rebound, on lingering concerns about the data centre operator's debt load.

Other neocloud firms Nebius Group ( NBIS ) and Iren ( IREN ) dipped over 2.8% each while chipmakers Micron Technology ( MU ) and Intel ( INTC ) fell 2.6% and 1.4%, respectively.

Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter, that some current Anthropic investors and prospective investors in its upcoming IPO are weighing a lower valuation, amid broader concerns over ballooning AI financing costs.

AI stocks have cratered this week as investors who have crowded into bets all along the AI supply chain worry that data centre operators might not turn profitable in time to repay debts, particularly with borrowing costs expected to rise.

Some of these stocks have risen sharply this year, helping push benchmarks S&P 500 and Nasdaq to record highs as recently as last week.

"When you've this incredibly bullish narrative matched with incredibly bullish outcomes but the stock declines, that is the sort of technical signal that tells you there's too many people in the pool," said James Athey, fixed-income portfolio manager at Marlborough.

The selloff in AI stocks sparked a rotation into defensive sectors such as healthcare on Thursday, helping the main indexes close slightly higher.

The S&P 500 and Nasdaq were set to post weekly losses as an AI-led rout, mixed earnings from big banks and inflation data weighed on sentiment through the week.

The Dow, however, remained on track for a weekly advance.

At 7:51 a.m. ET, Dow E-minis were down 20 points, or 0.04%, S&P 500 E-minis were up 3.5 points, or 0.04% and Nasdaq 100 E-minis were down 84 points, or 0.28%.

A nearly 1% fall in oil prices offered some support, though Brent crude remained above the $100-a-barrel mark.

Hotter-than-expected consumer and producer inflation reports this week have confirmed that price pressures are broadening out beyond energy products.

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh also noted that a spending surge was boosting inflation. He, however, said the US economy remained resilient and was benefiting from an AI-driven investment boom.

Markets increasingly expect the Fed to keep interest rates unchanged this month.

Among other movers, property-casualty insurer Travelers dropped 4% after reporting third-quarter results. Varonis Systems ( VRNS ) climbed 2.6% as Thoma Bravo's Proofpoint agreed to buy the data security firm in a $6.3 billion all-cash deal.

(Reporting by Tharuniyaa Lakshmi and Purvi Agarwal in Bengaluru, additional reporting by Vidya Ranganathan; Editing by Joyjeet Das)

data.title: US import prices increase more than expected in September
data.description:
WASHINGTON, Oct 16 (Reuters) - US import prices increased more than expected in September, boosted by higher costs for energy products and a range of other goods, further evidence of rising inflation pressures as the Middle East conflict persists.

Import prices jumped 1.1% last month after rebounding by a downwardly revised 0.5% in August, the Labor Department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said on Friday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast import prices, which exclude tariffs, increasing 0.8% after a previously reported 0.7% advance in August. 

In the 12 months through September, import prices rose 8.1%, the largest increase since July 2022, after increasing 6.7% in August. The government this week reported strong increases in consumer and producer prices, which left economists convinced that inflation was broadening beyond the energy sector. 

The dragging US-Israeli war with Iran has snarled supply chains, and is keeping oil prices elevated. 

Despite inflation heating up in September, financial markets still expected the Federal Reserve to skip raising interest rates later this month and tighten monetary policy in December.

The US central bank in September raised its overnight benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75%-4.00% range.

(Reporting By Lucia Mutikani; Editing by Chizu Nomiyama)

data.title: S&P 500 Correction Risk Grows as Index Rally Lacks Broad Participation
data.description:
08:18 AM EDT, 10/16/2026 (MT Newswires) -- With just a few high-flying technology names boosting the S&P 500 to record highs recently, many on Wall Street fear a potential correction, as the majority of index stocks have been hovering well below all-time peaks.

Only 10 stocks -- all beneficiaries of the ongoing artificial intelligence boom -- have driven 70% of the S&P 500's gain since March 30, The Kobeissi Letter, which provides insights on equity, commodity and bond markets, said in an Oct. 14 post on social media platform X.

The benchmark equity index weights companies using their total market capitalization, which means it is dominated by a handful of tech giants.

With Nvidia ( NVDA ) alone representing 8.4% of the S&P 500, a single company can influence index returns. Top 10 companies -- including Apple ( AAPL ) , Microsoft ( MSFT ) , Amazon ( AMZN ) , Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL) and Meta Platforms ( META ) -- account for nearly 40% of the index.

The S&P 500 futures were up 0.1% pre-bell Friday, though the benchmark is on track for a weekly loss. CoreWeave ( CRWV ) is down 15% for the week through Thursday amid investor concerns about the cloud-computing company's roughly $50 billion debt burden and the growing cost of artificial intelligence infrastructure.

The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite have rallied 13% and 15%, respectively, so far this year, having hit fresh closing highs Oct. 6. The Dow Jones Industrial Average is up 8.6% in 2026 through Thursday close.

But that rally hasn't been broad-based.

In fact, some 84% of S&P 500 companies sit at least 10% below their most recent peak, The Kobeissi Letter said in an Oct. 12 post.

A 10% stock pullback from recent highs is considered the minimum threshold for a market correction.

The real estate sector has apparently struggled the most amid high interest rates and rising materials costs, with 97% of its stocks down at least 10%, The Kobeissi Letter's analysis showed. That percentage is more than 90% each for materials, utilities, consumer discretionary and consumer staples.

Morgan Stanley Chief Investment Officer Mike Wilson has similar concerns about fewer stocks participating in the stock market rally, cautioning that a 5% to 10% correction at the S&P 500 index level could be in the cards if that gap remains unresolved.

The percentage of S&P 500 stocks trading above their 200-day moving average has fallen below 50% from about 75%, according to a transcript of Morgan Stanley's "Thoughts on the Market" podcast published Sept. 28.

"That divergence cannot persist forever," Wilson said on the podcast. "Either breadth catches up to price, or the index comes down to meet breadth."

An alternate measure that tracks the same set of S&P 500 companies, but assigns each constituent an equal, roughly 0.2% allocation shows a different picture than the standard market cap-weighted index.

The equal-weighed measure fell 2% in the third quarter, in contrast to a gain of the same magnitude at the standard S&P 500, Citadel Securities said in a report Oct. 1.

The S&P 500 Equal Weight index fell for seven straight weeks through the Sept. 27 week.

A pullback that has stretched this long has only been seen for "a handful of times" over the past three decades, and typically during bear markets, Liz Ann Sonders, chief investment strategist at the Schwab Center for Financial Research, said in a video published Oct. 7.

"Now, I would caution against reading that as some sort of precise signal, but it does tell you the average stock has been under more persistent pressure, week after week, with little relief, at least so far," according to a transcript of her video shared on Schwab Asset Management's website.

Sonders underscored the importance of "looking under the hood."

"If you only watched the (market cap-weighted) S&P 500 or the Nasdaq at the index levels, you would actually underestimate how painful this year has been for many individual stocks," she said.

The underlying weakness in equity markets has unfolded in the backdrop of elevated Treasury yields. The 10-year yield has risen nearly 80 basis points over the summer, J.P. Morgan Private Bank said in a report Oct. 2.

Higher bond yields raise stock investors' required rate of return, suppressing the present value of future cash flows. That would typically exert pressure on stocks because investors could, all else equal, get greater returns from relatively low-risk government debt.

"Whereas the majority of gains in the S&P 500 are driven by the heavyweight technology companies investing heavily in the AI build-out, other sectors that are less resilient are feeling the impact of higher (yield) rates," J.P. Morgan Private Global Investment Strategist Kriti Gupta said. "That even applies to sectors like utilities, which are exposed to the AI trade, but don't necessarily boast the same cash cushions or size as the hyperscalers."

If this bond volatility does not settle down soon, it could eventually drive the S&P 500 down by up to 10%, Morgan Stanley's Wilson said.

"Frankly, I would welcome it," he said. "A final index-level correction is often how a multi-month correction beneath the surface ends."

Earlier this year, Goldman Sachs cautioned that correction risks had increased, saying equity markets had become more vulnerable to disappointing economic news.

"There is a growing risk that rising bond yields, along with a slowing economy or inflationary pressures, could trigger a stock market correction," Goldman said in a report published in May.

A shrinking group of stocks lifting the S&P 500 has led Citadel to argue that the index doesn't fully capture broader market conditions.

"There is still plenty of stress beneath the surface," the brokerage said in the Oct. 1 report. The divergence between the S&P 500 rally and the average stock performance "highlights one of the most important features of this market: the stock market is not the economy, and increasingly, the S&P 500 is not the average stock."

data.title: Stocks Up Pre-Bell as Traders Parse President Trump's Latest Comments on Iran War
data.description:
08:02 AM EDT, 10/16/2026 (MT Newswires) -- The benchmark US stock measures were pointing higher before the open Friday as traders assess President Donald Trump's latest comments on the war with Iran.

The S&P 500 edged up 0.1%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 0.3% in premarket activity, while the Nasdaq 100 gained 0.1%. Equity markets finished the previous trading session in the green.

In an interview with Newsmax on Thursday, Trump said he isn't considering sending ground troops into Iran.

Trump's comments came after CNN reported, citing sources, that the US military has developed plans that include the potential use of a so-called "mother of all bombs" to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites.

"The mother of all bombs is not nuclear," Trump said in the Newsmax interview. "This is just an extremely large bomb."

Trump said the US may have to strike Iran's Pickaxe mountain, a suspected nuclear site, but he doesn't see ground troops being deployed for such an operation, Newsmax reported. The US leader also said Iran is negotiating with Washington and expressed confidence that the war in the Middle East "will be over very soon."

West Texas Intermediate crude oil decreased 0.6% to $97.39 a barrel early Friday, while Brent dipped 0.2% to $105.73.

The International Energy Agency on Thursday outlined plans to release more than 20 million barrels of diesel "as soon as possible" as part of its efforts to address a global supply crunch. In March, the agency agreed to release a record 400 million barrels of oil in a bid to stem crude prices and address supply disruptions triggered by the Middle East conflict.

Treasury yields were mixed, with the two-year rate retreating 0.5 basis points to 4.75% while the 10-year rate gained 1.3 basis points to 5.1%.

Government data showed Thursday producer prices jumped at the fastest pace in more than four years in September amid a surge in energy costs, a day after a report showed consumer inflation also accelerated last month.

Retail sales growth exceeded expectations in September as outlays at gas stations increased amid elevated fuel prices, the Census Bureau reported Thursday.

"With core inflation running at 2.6% year-on-year and oil prices remaining elevated, which increases the risk that price pressures spread to other categories, the (Federal Reserve) likely will not be able to remain on the sidelines for much longer," TD Economics Economist Admir Kolaj said in a Thursday note.

Despite the hot inflation reports, markets are currently pricing in an 85% probability that the Fed will keep its benchmark rate steady later this month, up from 72% on Thursday, according to the CME FedWatch tool. The remaining odds are in favor of a 25-basis-point hike.

Friday's economic calendar has the import and export prices report for September, followed by the industrial production report for the same month and the weekly Baker Hughes oil-and-gas rig count.

Travelers (TRV), Truist Financial ( TFC ) , M&T Bank ( MTB ) , Citizens Financial ( CFG ) and Regions Financial ( RF ) report their latest financial results before the bell.

Shares of Tesla (TSLA) jumped 4.3% pre-bell after the electric vehicle manufacturer unveiled its new Roadster car capable of flight using cold-gas thrusters. Nike ( NKE ) added 0.9% after closing the previous session with an increase of 5.2%.

J.B. Hunt Transport Services ( JBHT ) was down 1.3% as its third-quarter operating income as a percentage of revenue declined year over year.

Spot gold inclined 0.8% to $4,203 per troy ounce, while bitcoin traded down 0.3% at $82,080.

data.title: US Equity Futures Mostly Flat Pre-Bell as Fed Chair Kevin Warsh Avoids Interest Rate Guidance
data.description:
07:55 AM EDT, 10/16/2026 (MT Newswires) -- US equity futures were mostly unchanged pre-bell Friday as traders evaluated the lack of clues from Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh regarding another interest rate hike.

Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were flat, S&P 500 futures were up 0.1%, and Nasdaq futures were 0.2% lower.

At a fireside chat during the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Warsh declined to indicate the likely outcome of the Fed's October interest rate meeting while acknowledging the "synchronous tightening" by central banks around the world, CNBC reported.

The CME FedWatch tool showed the probability of the Federal Reserve raising its target rate by 25 basis points in October is at 16.1%, down from 27.7% on Thursday.

Traders also digested the latest round of corporate earnings, with Travelers (TRV) reporting higher core income and lower revenue for Q3.

Oil prices were higher, with front-month global benchmark North Sea Brent crude up 0.6% at $106.51 per barrel and US West Texas Intermediate crude 0.4% higher at $98.39 per barrel.

The September import price index, slated for 8:30 am ET, is expected to show a 1.0% month-over-month increase after a 0.7% gain previously, according to estimates compiled by Bloomberg. The export price index is projected to show a 0.9% increase, compared with a prior gain of 0.6%.

The September industrial production report, due at 9:15 am ET, is projected to show a 0.4% gain after holding steady in the prior month.
